entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Mesrop Mashtots (c. 361/362 – February 18, 440 AD) stands as the pivotal figure in the creation of the Armenian alphabet in 405 AD, an achievement that profoundly shaped Armenian national identity, literature, and the distinct character of the Armenian Apostolic Church. Operating amidst the geopolitical pressures exerted by the Sasanian Persian and Byzantine Empires on Armenia, Mashtots's linguistic innovation provided a unique cultural anchor, preventing the assimilation of the Armenian people into the dominant cultures of their powerful neighbors. His work was not merely an academic exercise but a strategic act of cultural preservation and empowerment, undertaken with the support of Catholicos Sahag I Parthev and King Vramshapuh.

Mashtots, initially a court secretary, embarked on his monumental task after recognizing the urgent need for a native script to translate the Bible and other Christian texts, as well as to facilitate widespread Christian education. Traveling to various centers of learning, including Edessa and Samosata, he meticulously studied different writing systems before devising the 36-letter Armenian alphabet. This new script was immediately employed to translate the Bible, completing the 'Holy Translators' movement, and soon after, Mashtots is also credited with creating the Georgian and Caucasian Albanian alphabets. His method involved careful phonological analysis to ensure a perfect fit between the spoken Armenian language and its written representation.
